questions.q: What was the immediate trigger for the Chipko Movement in 1973, and which group of villagers played the most visible role in the tree-hugging protests?
questions.a: The immediate trigger was the government’s auction of the Reni forest to commercial contractors in 1973; the most visible protesters were the women of Reni village led by Gaura Devi, who hugged trees to stop felling. A wrong answer (e.g., “men led the protests” or “it started against a dam”) reveals confusion with other movements or a failure to recall the specific gendered and localized nature of Chipko’s iconic action.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Ramachandra Guha describes the Chipko Movement as interlinking “red” (economic inequality) and “green” (ecological) issues.
questions.a: Guha argues that villagers depended on the forest for subsistence (firewood, fodder) — a “red” issue of livelihood inequality against commercial logging for profit — while deforestation caused floods and landslides, making ecological sustainability a “green” issue; for villagers, both were inseparable because their survival required the forest’s survival. A wrong answer that separates the two (e.g., “Chipko was only about saving trees”) misses the NCERT’s core argument that environmental movements in India fuse social justice and ecology.

questions.q: Apply the “old vs. new social movement” typology to the Chipko Movement: which features make it an “old” movement and which make it a “new” movement? Provide one specific example for each.
questions.a: Old: it involved a subsistence peasant/tribal community demanding livelihood rights (class-like economic grievance) — e.g., villagers needing firewood/fodder. New: it centred on ecological sustainability and local autonomy, cutting across class lines (women, villagers, urban supporters) and using novel symbols (hugging trees) — e.g., the movement’s emphasis on forests as ecological wealth for all. A wrong answer that labels it purely “old” or purely “new” fails to grasp the NCERT’s point that Indian movements blur this distinction.

questions.q: Analyze how the Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA) extended the Chipko template to the issue of large dams. Identify three specific parallels and one key difference in their mobilization strategies.
questions.a: Parallels: (1) both pitted subsistence economies (tribal/rural communities) against state-led “development” (commercial logging / large dams); (2) both linked ecological destruction (deforestation / submergence, salinity) to livelihood loss; (3) both challenged distant, unaccountable decision-making (plains-based government / central planning). Difference: NBA explicitly framed displacement as a violation of Adivasi constitutional rights (Fifth Schedule, PESA) and used legal PILs alongside mass satyagraha, whereas Chipko relied more on direct action and moral authority. A wrong answer that sees NBA as only a “dam opposition” without the rights/legal dimension misses its evolution of the ecological justice framework.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: “The Adivasi–environment linkage in Indian environmental movements is romanticized; in reality, Adivasis are often forced into destructive practices by poverty.” Use evidence from Chipko and NBA to support or refute.
questions.a: The statement is largely refuted by both movements: Chipko villagers protected forests despite poverty because their subsistence depended on intact ecosystems; NBA’s Adivasi leaders (e.g., Medha Patkar, Baba Amte) articulated a sophisticated critique of “development” that destroys both environment and culture. However, the critique holds partial truth where Adivasis are coerced into illegal logging/mining by lack of alternatives — a structural issue movements demand the state address. A wrong answer that uncritically accepts the “romanticization” charge ignores the movements’ own analysis of structural marginalization.

questions.q: Create a comparative table (mental or written) that maps the following dimensions for Chipko and NBA: (a) primary resource contested, (b) main social base, (c) key demand, (d) mode of protest, (e) outcome/legacy. Fill it with specific details from the NCERT and your knowledge.
questions.a: A good answer will produce a table with: Chipko — (a) oak/rhododendron forests, (b) hill villagers (esp. women), (c) stop commercial felling, community control, (d) tree-hugging, marches, cooperatives, (e) 15-year logging ban, inspired forest policies. NBA — (a) river Narmada / land for dams, (c) tribal/rural communities across three states, (c) halt dams, proper rehabilitation, rights-based development, (d) satyagraha, PILs, jal samadhi, international advocacy, (e) partial rehabilitation wins, Supreme Court rulings, global dam debate influence. A poor answer will leave cells vague (e.g., “forests” vs. “water”) or confuse the social base, showing inability to synthesize case details.
